newsitem.title: CHINA: Fate unclear for U.S. businessman jailed in China.
newsitem.headline: Fate unclear for U.S. businessman jailed in China.

text.p: A U.S. businessman began a 10-year sentence on Tuesday in a Chinese jail for smuggling garbage, with officials tight-lipped on whether they would force him to serve the term or free him to boost Sino-U.S. ties.
U.S. consular officials in Shanghai said they were seeking further information from Chinese authorities about how the courts planned to handle the case of William Ping Chen.

The Shanghai Number One People's Intermediate Court on Monday sentenced Chen, 56, to 10 years in jail, a fine of 500,000 yuan ($60,000) and deportation after convicting him of smuggling garbage into China.
It was not clear whether Chen would be immediately deported of whether he would be required to serve his jail term first.

Consulate officials said Chen still had the right to appeal and they had requested permission to visit him in jail. They refused to give further details of Chen's circumstances, saying he had demanded privacy.
In the past, China has frequently deported foreign nationals rather than face a potential diplomatic row.

But Chen's unusually harsh sentence was the climax of an emotional campaign launched by China in mid-1996 over illegal shipments of U.S. rubbish listed as waste paper for recycling but found to contain such items as old clothes, rubber gloves and disposable syringes.

China used the garbage issue to whip up anti-U.S. sentiment when relations with Washington had slipped to a low over a string of disputes ranging from U.S. charges of copyright piarcy in China to Beijing's anger over U.S. support for Taiwan.
Diplomats said Chen could have been unfairly singled out by China to make a diplomatic point.

However, the official Xinhua news agency said Chen had confessed to charges of smuggling a total of 238 tonnes of ordinary garbage and medical waste in 16 containers into Shanghai between July and December 1995.

Chen had listed the imports as waste paper and mixed paper, and gone ahead with the shipments despite warnings from the Shanghai Municipal Environmental Protection Bureau and opposition from his Chinese joint venture partners, it said.

Chen, who was arrested in June last year, was sentenced followed an open hearing on December 2 at which he was defended by two lawyers, Xinhua said. The hearing was attended by an official from the U.S. consulate in Shanghai.
The court verdict said Chen had evaded customs supervision to import the garbage and "had caused serious damage to the environment of China".
However, Chen could benefit from a warming in Sino-U.S. relations in recent months and from an agreement late last year on an exchange of presidential visits, the first since early 1989.
Analysts said it would make sense to remove the garbage factor to smooth the way for a possible visit to China in the first half of the year by U.S. Vice President Al Gore.
